Three things combine, all on `main` @ `276fbcff2`:

1. **`EngineCore.shutdown()` releases the structured-output backend first**, before it
   stops the executor and the scheduler — `vllm/v1/engine/core.py:812`:

   ```python
   def shutdown(self):
       logger.debug_once("[shutdown] EngineCore: tearing down local resources")
       self.structured_output_manager.clear_backend()   # ← released here
       if self.model_executor:
           self.model_executor.shutdown()
       if self.scheduler:
           self.scheduler.shutdown()
   ```

2. **`clear_backend()` destroys the backend but keeps the reference** —
   `vllm/v1/structured_output/__init__.py:484`:

   ```python
   def clear_backend(self) -> None:
       if self.backend is not None:
           self.backend.destroy()
           # self.backend is left pointing at the destroyed object
   ```

   `XgrammarBackend.destroy()` is `del self.compiler`
   (`vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py:169`). The other three backends'
   `destroy()` are `pass`, so only xgrammar leaves a half-destroyed object.

3. **The manager only ever builds a backend when the reference is `None`** —
   `__init__.py:141` (`if self.backend is None:`). Because step 2 leaves it non-`None`,
   the backend is never rebuilt, and `__init__.py:204`
   (`return self.backend.compile_grammar(...)`) uses the destroyed object.

Per-request error handling then works as designed — the `Future` carries the error so
only that request fails, not the engine. The defect is the message, and the fact that
the object can be used after it was released.

### What we saw

A client was issuing `json_object` requests in a loop when the server received
`SIGTERM`. Container log, same second throughout:

```
(EngineCore pid=111) INFO 10-11 00:42:27 [core.py:1332] [shutdown] EngineCore: trigger received signal=SIGTERM
(EngineCore pid=111) INFO 10-11 00:42:27 [core.py:1468] [shutdown] EngineCore: start mode=abort timeout=0s
(EngineCore pid=111) INFO 10-11 00:42:27 [core.py:1477] [shutdown] EngineCore: aborting in-flight requests count=1
(APIServer pid=1) INFO:     172.17.0.1:57796 - "POST /v1/chat/completions HTTP/1.1" 200 OK
(EngineCore pid=111) INFO 10-11 00:42:27 [core.py:1499] [shutdown] EngineCore: request processing complete; starting resource teardown
(EngineCore pid=111) INFO 10-11 00:42:27 [core.py:1345] [shutdown] EngineCore: exiting busy loop
(EngineCore pid=111) ERROR 10-11 00:42:27 [__init__.py:189] Failed to compile grammar for request chatcmpl-87db26a1efbd43b6-b431e330
(EngineCore pid=111) ERROR 10-11 00:42:27 [__init__.py:189] Traceback (most recent call last):
(EngineCore pid=111) ERROR 10-11 00:42:27 [__init__.py:189]   File ".../vllm/v1/structured_output/__init__.py", line 187, in _create_grammar
(EngineCore pid=111) ERROR 10-11 00:42:27 [__init__.py:189]     return self.backend.compile_grammar(request_type, grammar_spec)
(EngineCore pid=111) ERROR 10-11 00:42:27 [__init__.py:189]   File ".../vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py", line 86, in compile_grammar
(EngineCore pid=111) ERROR 10-11 00:42:27 [__init__.py:189]     ctx = self.compiler.compile_json_schema(
(EngineCore pid=111) ERROR 10-11 00:42:27 [__init__.py:189] AttributeError: 'XgrammarBackend' object has no attribute 'compiler'
```

Note the `200 OK` logged after `aborting in-flight requests count=1`: the API server was
still admitting and completing work while teardown ran.

## Steps to reproduce

1. `vllm serve <model>` (defaults; `auto` selects xgrammar).
2. Send `chat/completions` requests with
   `response_format: {"type": "json_object"}` in a loop.
3. `SIGTERM` the server (`docker stop`, `kill`, Ctrl-C, a container orchestrator
   draining the pod) while requests are in flight.

Not every attempt hits it — it needs a grammar request to reach `_create_grammar` after
`clear_backend()` has run. A graceful stop under load is an ordinary operation, so we do
not think this is an exotic condition; it is just a narrow window.

## Suggested fix

We have not sent a patch because the right shape is a maintainer's call. Three options,
smallest first:

1. Keep the state consistent: have `clear_backend()` set `self.backend = None` after
   `destroy()`. On its own this moves the failure to the
   `assert self.backend is not None` at `__init__.py:198`, which is not more legible —
   so it probably wants (2) with it.
2. Make the failure say what happened: mark the manager as released in
   `clear_backend()`, and in `_create_grammar` raise an error naming the cause
   ("the engine is shutting down; the structured-output backend has been released")
   instead of reaching the destroyed object.
3. Release the backend last: move `clear_backend()` in `EngineCore.shutdown()` after
   `model_executor.shutdown()` and `scheduler.shutdown()`, so nothing can still be
   scheduled when it goes. This narrows the window rather than closing it, and it is a
   teardown-ordering change, so we mention it but do not suggest it alone.

Happy to send a PR for whichever of these you prefer.

gh search issues --repo vllm-project/vllm "clear_backend"
gh search prs    --repo vllm-project/vllm "structured_output clear_backend"
```

The closest is #43920 (V1 structured outputs: a malformed grammar request after a valid
one crashes EngineCore) — same file, different mechanism: there the grammar is rejected
by a live compiler, here the compiler is gone. The most recent change to
`structured_output/__init__.py` is #59627 (2026-10-08), unrelated.

[Bug]: ECExampleConnector.has_cache_item() creates empty hash directories in shared storage on cache-miss lookups

### Summary

`ECExampleConnector.has_cache_item()` creates the hash directory in shared storage as a side effect of a **lookup**. Every cache-miss existence check leaves behind an empty `<mm_hash>/` directory, so the EC storage root accumulates one empty directory per unique hash that was ever checked but not cached. On multi-pod deployments this grows without bound and makes the shared EC cache impossible to inspect ("is this entry real or just a checked miss?").

### Mechanism (current `main`)

```python
# example_connector.py
def has_cache_item(self, identifier: str) -> bool:
    return self._found_match_for_mm_data(identifier)

def _found_match_for_mm_data(self, mm_hash) -> bool:
    """Check if the cache is hit for the request."""
    filename = self._generate_filename_debug(mm_hash)   # <- creates the folder
    return os.path.exists(filename)

def _generate_filename_debug(self, mm_hash: str) -> str:
    """...
    Ensures the parent directory exists because
    `_generate_foldername_debug` is called with its default
    (`create_folder=True`).          # <- the side effect is documented, but...
    """
    foldername = self._generate_foldername_debug(mm_hash)  # <- folder auto-created
    return os.path.join(foldername, "encoder_cache.safetensors")
```

The auto-creation is documented in the docstring, but the **lookup** path has no business creating anything: `has_cache_item()` is called

- from the scheduler on every encoder-input admission decision (`_try_schedule_encoder_inputs` → the "exists on remote encoder cache" check), and
- from `update_state_after_alloc()` on every multimodal allocation on consumer instances,

so one shared directory root ends up with an empty `<mm_hash>/` dir for **every image hash that was ever probed and missed**.

### Evidence (A100 EPD testbed, vLLM v0.30.0 — same code on `main`)

A single cache-miss probe (one direct request to the prefill instance carrying a new image, which the consumer-side `has_cache_item()` check missed) left this behind in the shared EC storage:

```
$ ls -la /shared/ec-cache/
drwxr-xr-x  2 root root 4096 ... 552b69fb8a152c7d3b57250ee6011c38595ef423efb2a1d871a646e68c602919   # empty, no encoder_cache.safetensors
drwxr-xr-x  2 root root 4096 ... 20ac77273f353d81f389c41fae2317ed72386b3b18264be77fd39665d383834a/  # real entry (has safetensors)
```

(The empty dir is the probe artifact from a checked-but-missed hash; the populated one is a real saved entry.)

### Impact

- Unbounded growth of empty directories in shared storage, one per unique missed hash, per deployment lifetime.
- `ls`-style inspection of the EC cache root can no longer distinguish "cached" from "was probed once"; ops tooling, backup/sync jobs and any GC based on directory listing get polluted.
- On network filesystems every probe becomes a metadata write.

### Suggested fix

Keep folder auto-creation on the **write** path (`save_caches`), disable it on the **lookup** path:

```python
def _found_match_for_mm_data(self, mm_hash) -> bool:
    filename = self._generate_filename_debug(mm_hash, create_folder=False)
    return os.path.exists(filename)

def _generate_filename_debug(self, mm_hash: str, create_folder: bool = True) -> str:
    foldername = self._generate_foldername_debug(mm_hash, create_folder=create_folder)
    return os.path.join(foldername, "encoder_cache.safetensors")
```

Three lines, no behavior change for saves. I'll follow up with a PR including a unit test asserting `has_cache_item()` does not touch the filesystem layout on a miss.

### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment (trimmed)</summary>

~~~text
vLLM 0.30.0 (official vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0 image), xgrammar 0.2.8 (upgraded from the bundled 0.2.7)
2x NVIDIA H200, CUDA image default, Python 3.12

vllm serve RedHatAI/Muse-Glimmer-30B-FP8-block \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer \
  --reasoning-parser muse_glimmer \
  --structured-outputs-config '{"backend": "xgrammar", "disable_any_whitespace": true}' \
  --generation-config auto --max-num-seqs 32 \
  --speculative-config '{"method": "dflash", "model": "<local dflash drafter>", "num_speculative_tokens": 15}'
~~~

The image also carries a port of #53404 (start the grammar at the `to=user` header, see #52594); without it the schema is not enforced at all on Muse.
</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `--reasoning-parser muse_glimmer` and a JSON schema (`response_format` / `structured_outputs.json`), the xgrammar bitmask allows Muse Glimmer's control tokens inside JSON strings: `<|eom|>` (200007), `<|start|>` (200022), `<|message|>` (200023) and the rest of the 2048 special added tokens (200000–202047), except the two stop tokens.

`XgrammarBackend` builds its `TokenizerInfo` with `xgr.TokenizerInfo.from_huggingface(tokenizer, vocab_size=...)`. xgrammar only treats tokens with an empty decoded string as special and ignores `added_tokens_decoder[...].special`, so for Muse `special_token_ids` comes back empty and every control token is an ordinary 7–11 character string the JSON string rule accepts.

When the model samples `<|eom|>` mid-string, the request still ends with `finish_reason=stop` and no error, but the `muse_glimmer` reasoning parser cuts `content` at that token, so the client receives JSON that ends inside a string (`EOF while parsing a string`). `<|start|>` / `<|message|>` / `<|reserved_special_token_N|>` end up as literal text in the JSON value instead.

Minimal reproduction on CPU, only the tokenizer is needed:

~~~python
import json, types
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from vllm.v1.structured_output.backend_types import StructuredOutputOptions
from vllm.v1.structured_output.backend_xgrammar import XgrammarBackend

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("RedHatAI/Muse-Glimmer-30B-FP8-block")

- `--long-prefill-token-threshold` capping per-step tokens below the item length (structural — that cap is applied to `num_new_tokens` before this guard runs).

step 1: scheduled={'text': 770, 'mm': 3}    mm_req: computed 0 -> 3     # (A) fires, correct rollback
step 2: scheduled={'text': 770, 'mm': 30}   mm_req: computed 3 -> 33    # <-- item chunked
step 3: scheduled={'text': 770, 'mm': 30}   mm_req: computed 33 -> 63   # <-- item chunked
step 4: scheduled={'text': 690, 'mm': 110}  mm_req: computed 63 -> 173  # <-- item chunked

I agree with @adityaanikam that `<=` is the safer of the two, and I have a concrete reason to keep (A) rather than delete it: its strict `<` is load-bearing for encoder-decoder models, by accident. Changing only `<` to `<=` makes three cross-attention tests in `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py` fail with an empty `scheduled_new_reqs` (`assert 0 == 3`):

- `test_cross_attn_blocks_not_over_allocated`
- `test_cross_attn_blocks_not_under_allocated`
- `test_variable_length_cross_attn_block_allocation`

For encoder-decoder models `start_pos` is only a marker (always 0) and `mm_position.length` is the encoder length, which is not part of the decoder token sequence — so the range arithmetic in this guard has no meaning there. `x < 0` was keeping those models out of the guard silently; `x <= 0` lets them in and rolls them back to zero tokens on every step. (Your stub sets `is_encoder_decoder=False`, so it cannot surface this.) So I think the guard wants an explicit `and not self.is_encoder_decoder` next to the `<=`.

### 3. A correction to the "cannot starve" argument

`compute_mm_encoder_budget()` validates `max_num_batched_tokens`, but nothing validates `long_prefill_token_threshold`. With `long_prefill_token_threshold=500` and `max_tokens_per_mm_item=576` (llava-1.5-7b) the per-step budget never grows, so:

- on `main` today the item is silently chunked (split at steps 2-3 in my trace), and
- with the `<=` fix alone the request gets 0 tokens every step, forever:

```text
step 1: scheduled={'text': 500, 'mm': 3}  mm_req: computed 0 -> 3
step 6: scheduled={'text': 500}           mm_req: computed 3 -> 3
step 7: scheduled={}                      mm_req: computed 3 -> 3   # engine idle from here on
step 8: scheduled={}                      mm_req: computed 3 -> 3
```

Also, the zero-token paths differ between the two call sites: the running-queue one does `continue` (`scheduler.py:567`), but the waiting-queue one does `break` (`scheduler.py:951`), so a waiting request stuck at zero additionally head-of-line-blocks the requests behind it.

Two ways to handle that configuration: keep chunking it (silently violating the flag), or reject it at startup. I lean towards rejecting, right next to the existing `max_num_batched_tokens` check, since the entire point of the flag is that the item is not split. The cost is real and worth stating: a configuration that combines a small `long_prefill_token_threshold` with `disable_chunked_mm_input` would go from "silently wrong" to "does not start".

### 4. Regression check

`tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py`: 147 passed before, 149 after (the two added tests). Whole `tests/v1/core` directory: 465 -> 467 passed with a byte-identical set of pre-existing failures on both trees (32 failed / 2 errors in my sandbox, all model-download or engine-spawning tests, unrelated to this change). Old code with the new tests fails exactly the two new ones (`mm item [3, 769) was chunked: 3 -> 33`, and `DID NOT RAISE ValueError`).

[Bug]: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash dsv4_topk Triton illegal memory access under high concurrency on H20; mitigated by max_num_seqs=256

### Summary

When serving `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` on 8x NVIDIA H20 (SM90), I can hit a CUDA illegal memory access in the Triton `dsv4_topk` MoE routing kernel under high concurrency when `max_num_seqs` is configured above 256.

Reducing `max_num_seqs` to `256` makes the deployment stable and the crash is no longer reproducible under the same workload.

This looks batch/sequence-size dependent rather than a generic GPU OOM or driver failure.

### Environment

- GPU: 8x NVIDIA H20 (Hopper / SM90)
- NVIDIA driver: `595.58.03`
- CUDA reported by `nvidia-smi`: `13.2`
- Model: `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` (mixed-precision deployment)
- Tensor parallel: 8
- Expert parallel: 8
- DSpark speculative decoding: enabled
- vLLM version/build: not present in the retained log excerpt; I can provide it if needed

### Error

The failing path is the MoE router's `dsv4_topk` Triton kernel:

```text
File "vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/router/fused_topk_bias_router.py", line 163, in fused_topk_bias
    return dsv4_topk(

File "vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/router/dsv4_topk.py", line 136, in dsv4_topk
    _dsv4_topk_kernel[(num_tokens,)](

RuntimeError: Triton Error [CUDA]: an illegal memory access was encountered
```

The exception propagates through `moe_runner.py -> router.select_experts() -> fused_topk_bias() -> dsv4_topk()` and causes worker/engine failure.

### Reproduction pattern

1. Serve DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on 8x H20 with TP=8 / EP=8 and DSpark enabled.
2. Configure `max_num_seqs` above 256.
3. Drive the server with high concurrent request load.
4. Eventually a worker crashes in `_dsv4_topk_kernel` with CUDA illegal memory access.
5. Change only the sequence concurrency cap to:

```bash
--max-num-seqs 256
```

6. Repeat the workload: the crash no longer reproduces.

I do not have the exact previous `max_num_seqs` value in the retained failing log excerpt, so I am intentionally not guessing it here. The important observed boundary/workaround is that `256` is stable while the higher setting was not.

### Expected behavior

Increasing `max_num_seqs` should not cause an out-of-bounds / illegal-memory-access failure in a routing kernel. If the kernel has a supported batch/token bound, vLLM should either handle/chunk the input or reject the configuration with a clear validation error.

### Notes / potentially related issues

- #51499 also reports an H20 / SM90 illegal-memory-access failure with DeepSeek V4, but that issue is in the DeepGEMM paged-MQA metadata path during CUDA graph capture. This report fails in the Triton MoE `dsv4_topk` routing path while serving under load, so it appears to be a different failure path.
- #49927 discusses `dsv4_topk` numerics/performance but not an illegal-memory-access crash.

### Questions

Could there be a missing bounds check or unsupported `num_tokens` / batch-size shape in `_dsv4_topk_kernel` when scheduler concurrency grows? Is there an intended upper bound for this kernel that should be reflected in scheduler/config validation?

I can provide a longer worker traceback and additional deployment/runtime details if useful.

[Bug]: an unclosed <tool_call> opener written in prose holds the Qwen3 parser in tool state and swallows a later genuine tool call

**Environment.** As in A (Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4, vLLM 0.28.0, `qwen3_coder`, template sha256 `0a20a467…abab9ab`).

**Describe the bug.** When the model mentions `<tool_call>` in prose without closing it — common when it explains or demonstrates the tool-call format — the state machine stays in tool state. Everything after is consumed as that span's body, including `</think>` and including a subsequent genuine tool call, which is therefore never emitted. The client receives a call named after the *first*, quoted block and does not receive the real one.

**Frequency.** 131 of 3,600 generations (3.6%) in our suite contain unbalanced `<tool_call>` markup (openers ≠ closers); 119 of those come from a prompt that asks the model to show the markup. At least one loses a genuine call as described.

**Concrete instance.** One generation, character offsets into the decoded output:

```
 2470  <tool_call>            <- opener, never closed
 2482  <function=function_name
 2890  <tool_call>            <- second opener, never closed
 4493  </think>
 4503  <tool_call>
 4515  <function=get_weather  <- the genuine call
 4586  </tool_call>           <- closes the span opened at 2470
```

The server returned `['function_name', 'get_weather', 'function_name']`; the final `function_name` is the span opened at 2,470 and closed at 4,586, and the real `get_weather` at 4,503 is inside its body. Replaying this through `Qwen3Parser` reproduces it exactly.

**Why the adjacent work does not cover it.** #56658 / #56661 add a function-header check before committing a span; this span *has* a header (`<function=function_name`), so that check confirms it rather than rejecting it. #50986 (`validate_tool_names`) drops the outer span because `function_name` is not offered — but the genuine call is inside that span's body and is dropped with it. Neither recovers the lost call.

**Suggested direction.** Bound how far a tool span may run — a turn-boundary or `</think>` token inside an open span is strong evidence the opener was prose, not markup — or reconsider the span at `finish()` when it never closed lexically. Raw generations available.

[Bug]: HunYuan Dense V1 fails CUDA graph capture on v0.29 — HF dynamic RoPE does a host-side sync during capture

### Your current environment

- vLLM 0.29.0 (official image), 2× L40S (also reproduces TP=1), transformers 5.16
- Model: hy-mt2-7b HunYuanDenseV1ForCausalLM checkpoint, `rope_scaling = {"type": "dynamic", "alpha": 1000.0, "factor": 1.0, ...}`, `max_position_embeddings=262144`


### 🐛 Describe the bug


### Reproduce
`vllm serve  hy-mt2-7b --tensor-parallel-size 2` (default `cudagraph_mode=FULL`).
vLLM downgrades to FULL_AND_PIECEWISE (FlashAttentionBackend, UNIFORM_BATCH), then dies during capture:

torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: operation not permitted when stream is capturing
  transformers/modeling_rope_utils.py:100  `if seq_len > max_seq_len_cached:`
  called from modeling_hunyuan_v1_dense.py:436 `position_embeddings = self.rotary_emb(...)`

### Root cause
Since #53615 the model runs on the Transformers backend. Dynamic-rope checkpoints go through
`@dynamic_rope_update`, where `dynamic_frequency_update` does
`seq_len = torch.max(position_ids) + 1; if seq_len > max_seq_len_cached:` — `Tensor.__bool__`
forces a D2H sync, which is illegal inside CUDA graph capture → capture invalidated
(cudaErrorStreamCaptureInvalidated at capture_end) → startup fails. Every cudagraph mode except
NONE fails (PIECEWISE capture passes 19/19 with torch.compile on, but the FULL phase /
profile_cudagraph_memory still runs the raw forward and dies).

Note: in vLLM `max_model_len <= max_position_embeddings`, so for these checkpoints the whole
dynamic update is a no-op — but the check itself still syncs.

### Regression
≤0.28 native `hunyuan_v1.py` computed the NTK-alpha inv_freq statically in `__init__`; CUDA graphs worked.

### Workaround
`--compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode": "NONE"}'` (starts, decode perf hit).

### Possible fixes
- In `vllm/model_executor/models/transformers/base.py`: bypass `dynamic_rope_update` when
  `max_model_len <= max_position_embeddings` (update is a no-op then), or
- warn + force `cudagraph_mode=NONE` for dynamic-rope models, or
- (upstream transformers) make `dynamic_frequency_update` capture-safe.

cc @hmellor (author of #53615)

[Feature]: Enable batch-sharded sampling for GPT-OSS

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Batch-sharded sampling was introduced in #50465, but GPT-OSS does not implement the required `compute_logits_local` interface. With Model Runner V2, enabling `--enable-batch-sharded-sampling` therefore logs a warning and falls back to regular sampling.

GPT-OSS uses the standard `ParallelLMHead` and `LogitsProcessor`, so it should be possible to enable the existing path by exposing rank-local logits with `skip_gather=True`.

This would allow GPT-OSS to distribute sampling work across TP ranks. In development benchmarks with GPT-OSS-20B on 2×L20, TP=2, and concurrency 256, enabling this path improved output throughput by approximately 4.5–6.0%.

### Alternatives

Continue using regular sampling. This works correctly but does not benefit from batch-sharded sampling.

### Additional context

The proposed change is limited to the model hook and regression coverage in the existing sharded-sampling E2E test. Logits redistribution and sampling remain handled by the shared runner.

Related: #56074, which addresses compatibility with lm_head LoRA.

[Bug]: sampler warmup misses the plain-greedy path — spec-decode rejection kernels JIT on the first request

Sibling of #54425 — same function, a second missing dimension. Filing separately because the
missing path and the observable failure are different; I have not touched that issue.

`SamplingParams.for_sampler_warmup()` is documented as "Set parameters to exercise all sampler
logic", but every warmup request gets `temperature=0.9`, so the warmup never takes the
`needs_logits_processing == False` early return in `Sampler.apply_sampling_params()` — the path
a plain `temperature=0` request uses.

With spec decoding that has a visible consequence. The startup warmup *does* reach
`rejection_sample()` (`_run_decode_step` populates `scheduled_spec_decode_tokens`), but it only
ever arrives there in fp32. dtype is a Triton compile key, so
`_compute_local_logits_stats_kernel`, `_rejection_kernel` and `_resample_kernel` are never
compiled for the model dtype and JIT on the first real greedy request:

```
startup (for_sampler_warmup) : needs_logits_processing=True  -> fp32
first temperature=0 request  : needs_logits_processing=False -> bfloat16   <- JIT here
```

`num_logits` is the same on both sides, so shape is held constant; warming the model dtype
alone takes the three `jit_monitor` warnings to zero. Measured first-request penalty on my box:
**+613 ms (52.1%)**. With `--jit-monitor-mode=error` the monitor is configured to raise on that
request (`vllm/utils/jit_monitor.py`), so this is not only a latency issue.

### The general shape (why this and #54425 are the same bug)

`warmup()` enumerates the **batch-shape** space carefully — `decode_steps`
(`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/warmup.py` L391-409 on main `@cacc429f6`) covers all-spec, mixed
spec/non-spec, single-request and no-draft-token variants, and L222-225 budgets for exactly
that (`num_decode_steps = 5 if num_spec_steps > 0 else 3`). But it samples the
**sampling-parameter** space at exactly one point — L280:

```python
sampling_params = SamplingParams.for_sampler_warmup()   # one object, all requests
```

#54425 is one axis of that point (no `seed` → FlashInfer is chosen, the seeded native
top-k/top-p + Gumbel path never runs). This report is another (`temperature=0.9` →
`needs_logits_processing` short-circuit never runs → the greedy dtype is never compiled).
Both are "the docstring says all sampler logic, and one dimension is pinned".

### Suggested fix

Same shape as #54425's: **run more than one sampler warmup configuration**, rather than
special-casing either axis. Concretely, either

1. add a second pass with a plain `SamplingParams()` (greedy) alongside the existing one, or
2. have `for_sampler_warmup()` return a small *list* of configurations and let `warmup()`
   iterate over it the way it already iterates over `decode_steps` (L409) — which would
   close #54425 and this one with the same change, and rides the structure already there.

I have a working local patch for the narrow greedy case (18 lines in
`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/warmup.py`) that takes the JIT warnings to zero, but it clears an internal
sampler buffer for the replay, which I don't think is the right shape to upstream. Happy to
send whichever of (1)/(2) you prefer as a PR.

### Environment

Intel XPU (Arc Pro B70), vLLM main `@cacc429f6` (2026-08-28), spec decode `qwen3_5_mtp`,
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MXFP4. I carry one unrelated local patch (an mxfp4 `register_fake`);
`sampling_params.py` and `warmup.py` are stock. No CUDA box here to confirm, and as far as I
can tell nothing in this path branches on platform, but I can't verify that claim on hardware.

### 🐛 Describe the bug ## Description For a BERT-style cross encoder, `padding="max_length"` pads `input_ids` correctly but assigns every padding token the last real token's `token_type_id`. In a query/document pair that value is normally 1, so padding is incorrectly treated as part of the document segment instead of using the tokenizer's `pad_token_type_id` of 0. BERT consumes token-type embeddings, so accepted `/score` and `/rerank` requests can run on different segment IDs from the tokenizer's intended input. This can change scores, rank order, and threshold decisions. ## Reproduction Use the script [repro.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32512913/repro_cross_encoder.py), run: ```bash python repro.py 2>&1 | tee reproducer.log ``` The reproducer uses vLLM's released rerank request, tokenization parameters, post-tokenization logic, and worker-side token-type compression. An in-memory BERT tokenizer provides the Transformers reference result, so no model download or GPU is required. The script exits with status 1 when the bug is reproduced. ## Actual result Both paths produce the same padded input IDs: ```text [2, 5, 3, 6, 3, 0, 0, 0] ``` vLLM produces: ```text token_type_ids = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] ``` ## Expected result Transformers uses the tokenizer's padding token type: ```text token_type_ids = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0] ``` Full log is here: [reproducer_cross_encoder.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32512950/reproducer_cross_encoder.log). ## Root cause `_apply_post_tokenization_to_token_type_ids()` pads with `token_type_ids[-1]` instead of `tokenizer.pad_token_type_id`. The following compression step stores only one zero-to-one boundary. That representation can encode `0*1*`, but not the correct right-padded shape `0*1*0*`, so the worker also reconstructs all padded positions as type 1. ## Related PR [PR #47772](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47772) fixes a different boundary problem after truncation. It does not change max-length padding or the single-boundary representation, so this case remains reproducible in vLLM 0.29.0. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

query:
[Feature]: Apply model-owned MTP shard selection to RunAI ModelStreamer

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Could `RunaiModelStreamerLoader` reuse the model-owned `is_unused_checkpoint_weight(name)` hook introduced by #60152, selecting safetensors shards **before** passing them to RunAI ModelStreamer?

#60152 now filters shards in `DefaultModelLoader`, but explicitly leaves RunAI unchanged. At inspected commit `705e124c05cffe7c00dd19434922c94e0610d674`, RunAI's `get_all_weights(model_config, model)` receives the model but passes only the weight source and revision to `_get_weights_iterator`. The latter sends the entire prepared file list to `runai_safetensors_weights_iterator`:

[Current RunAI loader](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/705e124c05cffe7c00dd19434922c94e0610d674/vllm/model_executor/model_loader/runai_streamer_loader.py#L135-L162)

Consequently, an opted-in MTP head does not get the same pre-read shard selection when using `--load-format runai_streamer`. Filtering tensors later in the model's `load_weights` does not prevent the streamer from receiving unnecessary shards.

**Proposed scope**

- Pass the existing, optional model-owned predicate into the RunAI loading path. Do not add architecture-specific naming rules to the generic loader.
- For local/Hugging Face-resolved safetensors, reuse `filter_safetensors_files_by_weight_name`.
- For S3/GCS/Azure sources, read only the checkpoint index metadata from the **actual weight URI**, including a `model_weights` override, and keep complete shards containing at least one required tensor. Do not assume the model-config cache directory contains the correct weight index.
- Keep mixed main/draft shards and unindexed additional files. Preserve the original path when no predicate or usable index is available; retain the existing all-rejected fallback.
- Leave tensor mapping, quantization, actual loading and model-specific rules with their existing owners.

This is **shard-level selection**, not tensor/range-level filtering inside RunAI. Mixed shards are still read in full. It does not imply that every MTP model is already opted into the hook, or that a model will benefit when every shard contains a needed tensor.

### Alternatives

#58016 addresses per-tensor skipping in the default lazy safetensors path, not RunAI.

#42060 / #48023 concern the draft's object-storage weight-source resolution. That correctness issue is separate from avoiding unnecessary reads and should not be folded into this optimization.

Hardcoding `mtp.` in RunAI would duplicate model-specific rules and miss differing checkpoint layouts; reusing #60152's hook avoids that.

### Additional context

I would be happy to contribute the implementation and regression tests. The intended validation includes main/draft-only and mixed shards, local and object-storage paths, missing/malformed indexes, unadapted models, and an independent `model_weights` source.

**Evidence status:** the missing hook connection is verified against the source above. No new RunAI end-to-end speedup or object-store byte reduction is claimed yet. Before a PR, I plan to compare unchanged and patched builds with identical configurations, recording main/draft loading times, readiness, selected files, generated outputs and draft acceptance.

I searched existing issues and open PRs for RunAI/MTP, the hook name, and references to #60152. I did not find an open PR covering this connection. AI assistance was used for source investigation and this proposal.

+
+For models exposing `is_unused_checkpoint_weight`, `runai_streamer` skips
+safetensors files containing only unused weights before streaming. It uses the
+same model-owned rule as the default loader, including MTP draft models with

+shards against their safetensors headers before streaming. Mixed shards remain
+included. Missing or inconsistent metadata retains the original file list.

+pipeline parallelism also retains the full file list. This optimization does

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Description

For a **bfloat16** model (e.g. `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`, which defaults to bf16), setting `kv_cache_dtype="float16"` is **accepted at config-validation time**, but the engine crashes later — during CUDA-graph capture / attention warmup — with a raw CUDA kernel assertion:

```
RuntimeError: mha_varlen_fwd, /workspace/.deps/vllm-flash-attn-src/csrc/flash_attn/flash_api.cpp:601, query and key must have the same dtype
```

Root cause: the FLASH_ATTN backend passes the **bf16 query** and the **fp16 key/value cache** straight into `flash_attn_varlen_func` without casting the query to the KV-cache dtype. The `mha_varlen_fwd` kernel requires `query`/`key` to share a dtype, so it asserts. Note the FLASHINFER backend does **not** have this problem — its log shows it resolves/casts the query dtype to match the KV cache (`FlashInfer resolved query dtypes: prefill=torch.bfloat16 ... kv_cache_dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn`), which is why the `fp8*` KV values all run fine. The crash is specific to the flash-attn path with a mismatched non-fp8 KV dtype.

This is a missing cross-field validation / missing cast: `CacheConfig._validate_cache_dtype` (`vllm/config/cache.py`) only emits an `info` log and never checks compatibility between `cache_dtype` and the model `dtype`; the attention backend selector likewise validates `kv_cache_dtype` against hardware/backend support *in isolation*, without reconciling it with the model's query/key dtype.

## Steps to reproduce

```python
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

llm = LLM(
    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct",  # config.torch_dtype = bfloat16
    dtype="bfloat16",
    kv_cache_dtype="float16",
    max_model_len=4096,
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.3,
    seed=42,
)
sp = SamplingParams(temperature=0.0, max_tokens=32)
llm.generate(["The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"] * 2, sampling_params=sp)
```

## Expected behavior

Either the engine works (cast the query to the KV-cache dtype, as the FLASHINFER path already does for `fp8`), or the incompatible combination is rejected cleanly at config-validation time with a descriptive error, e.g.:

```
ValueError: kv_cache_dtype="float16" is incompatible with dtype="bfloat16" on the FlashAttention backend.
```

Currently the mismatch is only discovered mid-warmup as a raw CUDA assertion.

## Actual behavior

Config accepted → engine loads weights → `profile_cudagraph_memory` → `capture_model` → `forward_fn(CUDAGraphMode.NONE)` → `unified_attention_with_output` → flash-attn `forward` → `torch.ops._vllm_fa2_C.varlen_fwd` → `RuntimeError`.

## Environment

- vLLM: 0.31.0 (official wheel)
- PyTorch: 2.13.0+cu130
- GPU: NVIDIA RTX A6000 (sm86), CUDA 13.0
- OS: Linux 6.8.0-138-generic, Python 3.12.13

## Additional context

- Found by a config-interaction test generator probing frontier enum values of `kv_cache_dtype` against a bf16 dense model.
- Cross-check of all 8 `kv_cache_dtype` values under the same model/seed:

  | kv_cache_dtype | outcome |
  |---|---|
  | auto / bfloat16 | OK |
  | **float16** | **RuntimeError: query and key must have the same dtype** |
  | fp8 / fp8_e4m3 / fp8_e5m2 | OK (routes to FLASHINFER; query dtype is resolved/cast to match fp8 KV) |
  | fp8_inc | `ValueError: No valid attention backend found` (separate, sm86 hardware-unsupported — not this bug) |
  | int8_per_token_head | OK (TRITON_ATTN) |

- The `fp8*` values working is the key evidence that the missing piece is a *query-to-KV cast / dtype-compat check on the FLASH_ATTN path*, not a fundamental bf16-vs-KV incompatibility: `fp8` KV is stored in `torch.float8_e4m3fn` while the query stays bf16, yet FlashInfer handles it.
- `CacheConfig._validate_cache_dtype` (`vllm/config/cache.py:337`) only logs an info string; it performs no compatibility check between `cache_dtype` and the model `dtype`. This is a missing cross-field validation of the same class as the `convert` × `runner` mismatch (separate issue): an invalid combination survives `EngineArgs.create_engine_config()` and only fails deep inside model init.

- The first failures appeared 6 minutes after the resume, and transfers were still failing at our last check, 22 minutes after it. We saw no recovery in that time. Restarting the group (46 minutes after the resume) fixed it.
- Lookups keep succeeding: the source reports holding the prefix (219-221 of 219-221 chunk lookups hit), so the router and engine keep choosing pulls that cannot succeed. Each one then hits issue 1 (a 30 s wait, then recompute).
- Pulls between the other three ranks keep working throughout.

UCX (`UCX_LOG_LEVEL=diag`) logged exactly one error on the paused rank, at the moment of `SIGCONT`:

```
04:56:27 ucp_ep.c:1905 UCX ERROR ep 0x7fc41735c100 has already been closed
```

That suggests the peers closed their UCX endpoints to it during the freeze.

Directed pulls 20-22 minutes after the resume, each a ~113K-token prefix warmed on the source and requested on the target with the source named in `kv_transfer_params.remote_kv_source`:

| Source → target | Bytes pulled | Tokens via P2P | Request time |
|---|---|---|---|
| healthy → healthy | 6.16 GB | 112,640 | 3.5 s |
| healthy → healthy | 6.16 GB | 112,640 | 3.3 s |
| healthy → **paused rank** | 0 | 0 | 37.1 s (recomputed) |
| **paused rank** → healthy | 0 | 0 | 37.3 s (recomputed) |

For contrast, blocking the P2P port on a rank with an iptables DROP for 3 minutes is handled correctly. Peers mark it down within 17 s, handshake retries are bounded (`no ConnectAckMsg within 30.0s`), and transfers work again after the block is lifted. The difference with `SIGSTOP` is that the paused process keeps its own NIXL/UCX state across the freeze, while its peers tear theirs down.

### Expected behavior

After a peer reconnects, P2P transfers to and from it work again. If the data path cannot be re-established, the peer should be treated as unavailable, so lookups MISS immediately instead of matching and then failing every fetch.

### Questions for maintainers

- On reconnect, are both sides expected to `remove_remote_agent` / `add_remote_agent` and rebuild the prepped descriptor lists? The paused rank was frozen while its peers declared it down, so its own view of them may never have been reset.
- Could NIXL be reusing a stale UCX endpoint when the remote agent of the same name is re-added? That would fit `ep … has already been closed` followed by `REMOTE_DISCONNECT` and then `NOT_FOUND`. If so, this may need a NIXL change or a fresh agent name or generation per registration.

### Reproduction

1. Two or more prefill ranks with the `p2p` secondary tier, under load that produces pulls.
2. `kill -STOP` one rank's EngineCore for longer than the peers' heartbeat timeout (10 s here; we used 45 s), then `kill -CONT`.
3. Wait for sessions to reconnect, then send a pull between the paused rank and a healthy one, in either direction.

We can provide full prefill logs, the UCX diag log of the paused rank, and py-spy stacks of all engine processes taken at the first failure.

Related: #60204 (why each failed pull costs the full timeout), #57139 (peer registration), #56836.

[Bug]: Scale-out token path breaks stop strings: stop text leaks into derendered output (include_stop_str_in_output ignored) and --tokens-only silently disables stop entirely

### Your current environment

Found by code inspection of `main` @ 2f46a1d9c6ab33c4ea8196c375ff85b661982bff while benchmarking the render/generate/derender flow (GKE, 1×A100-40G, Qwen3-8B). The paths below are reachable from reading the code alone; happy to attach `collect_env.py` output from the bench rig if useful.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Client `stop` strings are broken in two different ways on the scale-out token path (render → `/inference/v1/generate` → derender). Both are silent. Shared root cause: stop-string enforcement is a **text-level** operation inside the engine's incremental detokenizer, but the scale-out protocol transports **token IDs**, which the detokenizer deliberately never truncates.

#### Bug A — stop-string text leaks into derendered output; `include_stop_str_in_output=False` is silently ignored

On a scale-out generate host **without** `--tokens-only`, stop strings do fire engine-side: the detokenizer matches and truncates `output_text` (`vllm/v1/engine/detokenizer.py:132-141`) and the request finishes with `finish_reason="stop"`. But:

- Token IDs are never truncated — even the token excluded from detokenization when `include_stop_str_in_output=False` is appended back to `self.token_ids` (`vllm/v1/engine/detokenizer.py:111-127`). This is by design; only the *text* is cleaned.
- `ServingTokens` builds its response from the full token ID list and discards the engine's truncated text (`vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/serving.py:326` batch, `:451` streaming).
- The derenderer decodes every token it receives (`vllm/renderers/online_derenderer.py:126`, `:189`, `:413`, and the `_detokenize_delta` streaming path). `include_stop_str_in_output` and `check_stop_strings` are referenced **nowhere** under `vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/` or in `vllm/renderers/online_derenderer.py` (grep confirms zero hits).

Result: a request with `stop=["\n\n"]` returns clean truncated text from a coupled `vllm serve` server, but through render → generate → derender the client receives the stop string — plus any partial text decoded past the match point — embedded in `content` / `text`. This contradicts the parity promise in `docs/serving/online_serving/derenderer.md` ("the same output as a standard `vllm serve` server").

**Update 2026-09-30** (independent A/B by @Yunzez, https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/57052#issuecomment-5918028677, verified against `main`):

- Reproduced with no parser on a plain `vllm serve` host across chat batch, completions batch and chat streaming, on 0.27.1 and 0.29.0. Same token count and `finish_reason="stop"` on both paths; only the stop handling differs.
- **`stop_token_ids` leak the same way.** The detokenizer skips the stop token for text but appends its ID back to `token_ids` (`detokenizer.py`, `skipped_stop_token_id`), so derender decodes it. This needs a token-level rule, not a text scan: if `finish_reason == "stop"` and the last token is in the request's `stop_token_ids`, drop it before decoding unless `include_stop_str_in_output`.
- **`stop_reason` is `null` on every derendered response.** `GenerateResponseChoice` has no such field and `online_derenderer.py` builds both chat and completion choices with `finish_reason` only; the coupled routes fill it from `output.stop_reason`. #47313 adds `stop_reason` to the generate response (open, mergeable, marked stale 2026-09-30).

Repro sketch (no GPU-specific behavior involved):

1. `POST /v1/chat/completions/render` with a request containing `"stop": ["<some string the model will emit>"]`.
2. Forward the `GenerateRequest` to `/inference/v1/generate` on a scale-out host.
3. `POST /v1/chat/completions/derender` with the `GenerateResponse`.
4. Compare `choices[0].message.content` with the same request against a coupled server: the derendered content ends with the stop string; the coupled content does not.

#### Bug B — `--tokens-only` hosts silently never apply stop strings at all (**fixed in #57058**)

`SamplingParams` validation rejects `stop` with `detokenize=False` (`vllm/sampling_params.py:650-656`, "stop strings are only supported when detokenize is True"). But on a `--tokens-only` host, `ServingTokens` sets `sampling_params.detokenize = False` **after** the request has already passed validation (`vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/serving.py:224-225`), so the guard never sees the combination. Downstream, the tokenizer-less base `IncrementalDetokenizer.update` never calls `check_stop_strings` (`vllm/v1/engine/detokenizer.py:31-44`).

Result: generation runs to EOS or `max_tokens`. No error, no warning, no log line. The failure is easy to miss in production because `stop_token_ids` still work (they need no detokenization), so a deployment can look healthy while `stop` strings specifically do nothing — burning decode time and returning over-long outputs that then also hit Bug A's leak on the derender side.

#### Test gap

Nothing under `tests/entrypoints/scale_out/` mentions `stop`, `include_stop_str_in_output`, or stop truncation, and the derender parity test round-trips a coupled response's already-clean fields, so neither bug is observable there.

#### Proposed fix (willing to submit PRs)

1. ~~**Fail loud on Bug B**~~: done in #57058 (`--tokens-only` returns 400 on `stop`).
2. **Bug A**: the derenderer already receives the original `chat_request` / `completion_request`, which carry `stop` and `include_stop_str_in_output`. After decoding, apply `check_stop_strings` (reusing `vllm.v1.engine.detokenizer.check_stop_strings`, not a reimplementation) and truncate the decoded text — batch first; the streaming path needs the hold-back buffer, which `DerenderStreamState` can carry alongside the detokenizer state it already threads through. Token IDs stay untruncated at the generate host, matching the coupled engine's semantics and keeping token-out consumers (RL) whole.
   - Alternative considered: ship truncation info (matched stop / truncation offset) in the generate protocol instead. That overlaps with #47313 (adding `stop_reason` to generate response choices) and would want coordination there.
   - **Status 2026-09-30:** batch is still unowned. The batch pass should also apply the `stop_token_ids` token rule above and set `stop_reason` (pass-through once #47313 lands, or computed from the match). For streaming, the direction agreed on #47161 is to reject `stop` on streaming `/derender` with a 400 for now; the engine-side fix is `output_mode` (#56851), where the engine's own hold-back applies and the text arrives already truncated.
3. Tests: a stop-string case in `tests/entrypoints/scale_out/derender/test_derender_parity.py` asserting coupled == derendered, and a `--tokens-only` case asserting the 400.

Feedback welcome on 2 — derender-side re-matching vs. protocol change is a real design fork.

#### Related

- #56993 mentions the `--tokens-only` stop-string silence in passing as motivation for the component split, but proposes launch-surface restructuring rather than a fix; Bug A is not covered there or anywhere else I could find.
- #46310 rejects `stop` when `skip_tokenizer_init` is set, but guards a different layer and does not catch the post-validation `force_no_detokenize` assignment above.
- #56851 notes "stop strings need detok" when discussing skipping detokenization on tokenizer-loaded generate servers (out-of-scope section).
- #51641 / #36983: stop-buffer `delta_text`/`delta_token_ids` desync — relevant to the streaming hold-back design in fix 2.
- #47313: `stop_reason` on `/inference/v1/generate` responses (needed for `stop_reason` parity on derender).
- #47161 / #56851: streaming direction (reject `stop` on streaming `/derender`; `output_mode` applies stop engine-side).

[Bug]: CPU backend KV cache sizing error reports a negative size and recommends the wrong fix

### Your current environment

- vLLM `main` at `fc2c801ad9` (2026-09-30), CPU backend built from source
- macOS 27.0, Apple M1 (arm64), 8 GiB RAM, torch 2.13.0, Python 3.12
- The code path is platform-independent (`vllm/v1/worker/cpu_worker.py`)

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When the CPU worker's own footprint (model weights plus runtime) is larger than the memory reserved by `--gpu-memory-utilization`, startup fails with an error that contradicts itself and recommends the wrong fix:

```
ValueError: Available memory on node 0 (1.34/8.0 GiB) on kv cache allocation is less than requested memory for kv (-0.6/0.16 GiB). Reduce CPU memory used by other processes.
```

- It reports a **negative** KV request (`-0.6 GiB`) and calls 1.34 GiB "less than" it.
- The advice, "reduce CPU memory used by other processes", can't help: this worker has already used up its own reservation. What works is a larger `--gpu-memory-utilization`, or an explicit `--kv-cache-memory-bytes` / `VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE`.
- On a machine with little free RAM, the startup check tells users to *decrease* `--gpu-memory-utilization`. Following that advice leads straight into this error, which then points somewhere else again.

Reproduction (default multiprocess engine):

```python
from vllm import LLM

if __name__ == "__main__":
    LLM(model="HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M", dtype="float32", max_model_len=512,
        enforce_eager=True, gpu_memory_utilization=0.02)
```

With `gpu_memory_utilization=0.01` the error reads `(-0.46/0.08 GiB)`.

**Cause.** In `CPUWorker.determine_available_memory` (`vllm/v1/worker/cpu_worker.py:237-249`), `requested_memory_for_kv = requested_cpu_memory - rss`. The two failure conditions, `requested_memory_for_kv <= 0` (the worker outgrew its reservation) and `requested_memory_for_kv > available_memory` (the node is short of free memory), share one message. That message only fits the second case.

#42479 reworded the neighbouring CPU memory errors but did not touch this branch. Related: #29233.

[Bug]: DSpark scheduling using an overly conservative input budget ### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text Your output of `python collect_env.py` here ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug The scheduler charges each DSpark request `num_new_tokens + K - 1`, where `K` is `num_speculative_tokens`. However, the target/context tokens and the fixed-size draft query block are processed in separate stages. Combining them into one budget can unnecessarily restrict scheduling. For example, assume: ```text max_num_batched_tokens = 16 num_speculative_tokens = 4 2 requests, each scheduling 8 prefill tokens ``` Both requests fit the two stages: ```text target/context stage: 8 + 8 = 16 tokens DSpark query stage: 4 + 4 = 8 tokens ``` Current accounting charges `8 + (4 - 1) = 11` for the first request, so the two requests cannot be admitted in full despite fitting both stages. This may also affect other speculative methods. A possible fix is to keep target and draft-input budgets separate, with each method defining its draft-stage input cost. We may be missing some intended scheduling semantics; we are validating this experimentally and exploring a fix. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

I looked into this and I think the combined accounting is intentional rather than an over-restriction, so I wanted to lay out the evidence before anyone changes it.

The premise in the report is that the target/context tokens and the draft query block are processed in separate stages and can therefore be budgeted separately. The code suggests they land in the *same* batch, and that `input_budget` is precisely the capacity of that single batch.

**1. `max_num_scheduled_tokens` exists specifically because the model appends draft tokens to the same batch** (`vllm/config/scheduler.py`):

> Maximum number of tokens that the scheduler may issue in a single iteration.
> This is usually equal to `max_num_batched_tokens`, but can be smaller in cases **when the model might append tokens into the batch (such as speculative decoding)**.

So the scheduler deliberately issues fewer tokens than the batch can hold, reserving the remainder for what drafting will append.

**2. `max_num_new_slots_for_drafting` is documented as slots within that same budget** (`vllm/config/speculative.py`):

> Return the maximum **additional** drafting slots per request.
> **The scheduler budget already includes one query slot per decoding request.**

and for DSpark specifically:

> The existing query is reused; only masked queries need new slots. → `K - 1`

The notions of "reusing the existing query slot" and needing "additional slots" only make sense if draft and target queries occupy one shared budget. If drafting had its own independent budget, DSpark would need `K`, not `K - 1`.

**3. The config-time error message says the same thing** (`vllm/config/vllm.py`, `_set_max_num_scheduled_tokens`):

> Increase `max_num_batched_tokens` **to accommodate the additional draft token slots**, or decrease `num_speculative_tokens`.

Under that reading, the walked-through example behaves as intended: with `max_num_batched_tokens=16` and `K=4`, admitting both 8-token prefills would make the realized batch `16 + 2*(K-1) = 22` tokens, exceeding the configured batch capacity. Charging `8 + 3` per request keeps the realized batch within 16.

That capacity is not merely advisory — `max_num_batched_tokens` feeds CUDA graph capture sizes in `_set_cudagraph_sizes`, so exceeding it at runtime risks a shape miss rather than just extra memory use.

**Where I could be wrong:** if DSpark's draft block really is a separate forward pass with its own allocation, none of the above applies and separate budgets would be right. I could not find that separation in the scheduler or the config layer, but I have not traced the DSpark model runner path end to end, and I have no DSpark checkpoint to measure with.

So the concrete question for @maintainers is whether the DSpark draft block shares the target batch (in which case the current accounting is correct and this can be closed) or is genuinely a separate forward (in which case the fix should also revisit `max_num_scheduled_tokens` and the CUDA-graph sizing, not just the per-request charge).

Happy to help verify empirically if someone can point me at a DSpark config that fits on a single H20.

hints:
The guard is stricter than the constraint it protects, and the difference is checkable from the
model config — no special hardware needed. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next we have been running `-pp 2`
since 2026-08-30 with a conditional relaxation, and we read the output rather than only timing
it.

### The constraint vs. the guard

```
NotImplementedError: Qwen4Exp N-gram PLE embedding requires pipeline_parallel_size=1
because non-first pipeline ranks do not receive the raw input_ids it needs.
```

The reason is real, but it only bites when a PLE layer actually lands on a non-first rank. Which
layers those are is named in the config:

```
num_hidden_layers = 48
ple_layer_ids     = [2]
```

With `pp_size = 2`, rank 0 holds layers 0–23, so layer 2 — the only consumer of raw `input_ids` —
is on the first rank, and the situation the guard protects against does not arise.

The same holds for the configuration in this report. `get_pp_indices(48, 0, 3)` gives rank 0
layers 0–15, so `--pipeline-parallel-size 3` puts layer 2 on the first rank as well — the
predicate below would admit it. (We have only run `pp_size = 2` on our own hardware.)

So the check that matches the constraint is not `pp_size > 1`, but *"do all `ple_layer_ids` fall
on the first stage?"* — asked with the same function the model itself uses to decide which layers
it owns:

```python
from vllm.distributed.utils import get_pp_indices

if text_config.ple_layer_ids and parallel_config.pipeline_parallel_size > 1:
    start, end = get_pp_indices(
        text_config.num_hidden_layers, 0, parallel_config.pipeline_parallel_size
    )
    if not all(start <= int(i) < end for i in text_config.ple_layer_ids):
        raise NotImplementedError(...)   # message unchanged
```

Asking `get_pp_indices` rather than recomputing the split matters: `VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION` can
override the partition arbitrarily (only its length and sum are validated), so
`VLLM_PP_LAYER_PARTITION="1,47"` would put layer 2 on rank 1 while any `num_layers // pp_size`
arithmetic still said "first stage". **A model whose PLE layers do land on a later rank keeps
raising, exactly as today** — that is the point of making it a predicate rather than lifting it.

We only have Flash-Next's config on hand, so we are not claiming every Qwen4Exp layout is safe.
We are claiming the opposite: some are not, and a predicate is what tells them apart.

### One practical note for whoever fixes this

The same premise is asserted in three places, and the one in `config.py` fires first — before the
weights are read:

| file | |
|---|---|
| `model_executor/models/config.py:879` | `NotImplementedError`, fires earliest |
| `models/qwen4_exp/nvidia/model_state.py:35` | `RuntimeError` |
| `models/qwen4_exp/amd/model_state.py:35` | identical to the nvidia copy |

They all state the same condition, so the fix is one predicate rather than three — but it has to
include the one in `config.py`. We patched the model-side checks first and were still blocked.

### What it unblocks

For the reporter of this issue, PP is how the model fits at all. On our box it also changes what
speculative decoding is worth. Measured against each configuration's own no-speculation baseline
(slope of wall-clock at 80 and 480 tokens, n=5 median, output read each time):

```
-pp 2 :  K=2 speculative decoding   −32.7% per token
-pp 1 :  K=2 speculative decoding   −16.0% per token
```

We give ratios rather than absolute numbers because the two were measured in different sessions
and this box drifts ~5.7% between runs; each ratio's numerator and denominator come from the same
session. The acceptance curve also has a minimum that is not at the highest acceptance: K=1
accepts 80.6% but is slower than K=2 at 67.1%.

### Relation to #50514

#50514 took the general route for the equivalent problem on the other side of the pipeline: the
draft ids existed only on the rank that produced them, and the fix was to add the wire. The same
route would lift this condition entirely, by making raw `input_ids` available to any rank. The
conditional check above is the cheaper step in the meantime, and it costs nothing if the wire
lands later.

Happy to open a PR with the predicate. One caveat on scope: it touches
`models/qwen4_exp/{nvidia,amd}/model_state.py`, and we can only exercise the XPU path here — we
would need someone to confirm CUDA and ROCm.

### Disclosure

Intel Arc Pro B70 ×2 / vLLM-XPU, which upstream CI does not cover. The config values above are
readable from the public checkpoint and the partition behaviour from `vllm/distributed/utils.py`,
so the argument does not depend on our hardware; only the speed numbers do. We carry local
patches for UVA weight offload and an expert VRAM cache; neither touches the PLE path.

[Bug]: V2 block verification (rejection_sample_method="block") reuses position-keyed uniforms across rounds, so sampled output is biased ### Your current environment
Environment (from the run logs; collect_env.py was not captured on that machine) ```text vLLM 0.31.0, torch 2.13.0+cu130, Python 3.12 GPU: Tesla T4 (sm_75), driver 580.82.07 (Colab), V2 model runner Kernel-level check also run on main 1dfe9fbdae73 under TRITON_INTERPRET=1 (triton 3.8.0, torch 2.13.0+cpu) ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug With the V2 runner, `rejection_sample_method="block"` and temperature > 0, the sampled output does not follow the target model's distribution. Standard verification on the same setup is fine. The acceptance uniform is `tl_rand32(seed, pos)` with one seed per request and the absolute position. In block mode every draft row reads its uniform, including rows after the accepted length. Those uniforms have been conditioned on that round's decision, and the next round verifies the same positions again with the same uniforms. A small case: the target is p = (1/2, 1/2) at every position, the drafter always proposes token 0, and gamma = 2. The third generated token is 0 with probability 5/12 instead of 1/2. The script below calls the V2 `rejection_sample` round by round with the inputs the model runner builds (rows `[last committed, d_1, d_2]` at positions `[L-1, L, L+1]`), so no model is needed: ```python import argparse import torch from vllm.v1.worker.gpu.spec_decode.rejection_sampler_utils import rejection_sample def run(block, fresh_seed, n_req, n_tok=6, gamma=2, p0=0.5, base_seed=12345, device="cuda"): logp = torch.log(torch.tensor([p0, 1 - p0], dtype=torch.float32)) g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(base_seed) out = [[int(torch.rand((), generator=g) >= p0)] for _ in range(n_req)] # prefill token seeds = torch.randint(0, 2**31 - 1, (n_req,), generator=g, dtype=torch.int64) rnd = 0 while True: active = [r for r in range(n_req) if len(out[r]) < n_tok] if not active: break rows, n = gamma + 1, len(active) L = torch.tensor([1 + len(out[r]) for r in active]) # prompt length 1 target_logits = logp.repeat(n * rows, 1).contiguous() draft_sampled = torch.zeros(n * rows, dtype=torch.int64) # drafts are always 0 pos = torch.zeros(n * rows, dtype=torch.int64) for k, r in enumerate(active): draft_sampled[k * rows] = out[r][-1] pos[k * rows:(k + 1) * rows] = torch.arange(L[k] - 1, L[k] - 1 + rows) cu = torch.arange(0, (n + 1) * rows, rows, dtype=torch.int32) idx_mapping = torch.arange(n, dtype=torch.int32) expanded_idx = idx_mapping.repeat_interleave(rows) expanded_local = torch.arange(rows, dtype=torch.int32).repeat(n) temperature = torch.ones(n, dtype=torch.float32) seed = seeds[active].clone() if fresh_seed: seed = (seed * 1000003 + 7919 * (rnd + 1)) % (2**31 - 1) args = [t.to(device) for t in (target_logits,)] + [None] + [ t.to(device) for t in (draft_sampled, cu, pos, idx_mapping, expanded_idx, expanded_local, temperature, seed)] sampled, num_sampled = rejection_sample(*args, gamma, use_block_verification=block) sampled, num_sampled = sampled.cpu(), num_sampled.cpu() for k, r in enumerate(active): out[r].extend(int(t) for t in sampled[k, : int(num_sampled[k])]) rnd += 1 return [sum(o[j] == 0 for o in out) / n_req for j in range(n_tok)] def main(): ap = argparse.ArgumentParser() ap.add_argument("--device", default="cuda") ap.add_argument("--n-req", type=int, default=100000) a = ap.parse_args() for block, fresh in [(False, False), (True, False), (True, True)]: m = run(block, fresh, a.n_req, device=a.device) name = f"{'block' if block else 'standard'}, {'fresh' if fresh else 'fixed'} seed" print(f"{name:22s} P(token j = 0), j = 0..5:", " ".join(f"{x:.4f}" for x in m)) print("exact: 0.5 at every j") if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` On a T4 with 10^6 requests I get: ```text standard, fixed seed P(token j = 0), j = 0..5: 0.5012 0.5000 0.5001 0.4999 0.4994 0.5005 block, fixed seed P(token j = 0), j = 0..5: 0.5012 0.5003 0.4167 0.4862 0.4694 0.4661 block, fresh seed P(token j = 0), j = 0..5: 0.5012 0.5006 0.5005 0.4989 0.5008 0.4998 exact: 0.5 at every j ``` "fixed seed" is what the runner does (one seed per request). Changing only the seed every round removes the bias, so the cause is the reuse of the position-keyed uniforms. Token 0 is the prefill token, which doesn't go through verification. On main 1dfe9fbdae73 under the Triton interpreter (20000 requests) I get the same pattern: .506 .498 .415 .486 .461 .466, which is 24σ off at the third token. End to end it shows up the same way. With a tiny context-free model (p = (1/2, 1/2)), a draft model that always proposes the same token, gamma = 2 and 10000 samples on the T4, block verification rejects the correct output law (chi-square 3152, df 64, p ≈ 0) and fits the law the kernel above predicts (p = .48), while standard verification on the same models fits the correct law (p = .87). With probabilistic drafts (p = (.3, .7), q = (.7, .3)) block mode gives P(third token = a) = .3509 instead of .30. With the same kernel and freshly drawn drafts it is .3003 there, so in that case the extra bias comes from the draft Gumbel noise, which is keyed the same way by (seed, position). That is why only block mode is affected. Related: #47386 (closed) noted in its description that re-proposals at the same position reuse that position's draft key across steps, and #54282 decoupled the draft and target noise within a round. Neither covers the acceptance uniform in block mode. Suggested fix: it might be enough to mix something that changes every verification step into the uniform's offset (for example a per-request step counter), and the same for the draft noise. In the script, a fresh seed per round is exact. --- AI-assisted: found, reproduced and written up with Claude.

[Feature]: Logprobs on parsed path streaming `/derender`

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Streaming `/derender` with a reasoning or tool parser (#50550) doesn't return logprobs. #55029 added streaming logprobs but only on the unparsed path. The parsed path builds its stream choices without them. A client that streams with `logprobs: true` through a parser gets nothing back.

Agreed on #47161 (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47161#issuecomment-5893681568): the engine is the reference for logprob token strings. Standalone `/derender`, including the parsed path should use one shared resolver built on `convert_ids_list_to_tokens` and `_correct_decoded_token` with parity tests against the engine.

Scope:

- Resolve each chunk's logprobs and attach them to whatever delta the parser emits. `/v1/chat/completions` does the same, with one `logprobs.content` list no matter which field the tokens land in.
- Update `logprob_context_token_ids` on the parsed path, like the plain path does. Keep it starting empty, like the engine.
- Drop logprobs on every chunk when `include_reasoning=false` with a parser, like the engine does.
- Fix batch derender too. `_derender_chat` clears `reasoning` but still returns the logprobs.
- Add parity tests against `/v1/chat/completions` with `include_reasoning` on and off, a chunk the parser swallows (tool-call markup) and a multi-byte char split across chunks.

`DerenderStreamState` stays as is. Chunk logprobs already cover only that chunk's tokens and replay never touches them, so no cursor is needed. #59510 handles streaming stop with a 400, so no pending text field either.

Blocked on #58181 (still open). The shared helper (`decode_token_ids`) and the parity tests depend on it.

@shimib has offered to take this. @hyeongyun0916 will review and help with repros.

### Alternatives

Re-resolving token strings separately in the parsed path. We ruled this out on #47161 because the paths already disagree (see #59241).

### Additional context

- #47161: RFC thread where this was agreed
- #55029: streaming logprobs for the unparsed path
- #50550: parser aware streaming derender
- #58181 / #57574: `GenerateLogProbs` with integer token IDs
- #59241 / #59252: SentencePiece leading space dropped in derender logprob strings
- #57052 / #59510: stop handling on derender. #59510 makes streaming `/derender` return 400 on `stop` and notes that logprobs aren't trimmed to the cut text.

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

+def _logprob_tokens(choice: dict) -> list[tuple[str, list[int] | None]] | None:
+    lp = choice.get("logprobs")
+    if lp is None or lp.get("content") is None:
+        return None
+    return [(e["token"], e.get("bytes")) for e in lp["content"]]
+
+
+def _sampled_generate_logprobs(choice: dict) -> dict | None:
+    """`GenerateLogProbs` for one coupled stream chunk from its `token_ids`
+    and per-token logprob values, without `top_logprobs`.
+
+    The coupled stream's `token_ids` are the integer ids a GPU-less worker
+    would have sent, so one stream is both the derender input and the string
+    reference. A second greedy run is not needed, and greedy decoding is not
+    bit-reproducible across calls on every platform anyway.
+    """
+    lp = choice.get("logprobs")
+    if lp is None or lp.get("content") is None:
+        return None
+    content = lp["content"]
+    assert len(content) == len(choice["token_ids"]), choice
+    return {
+        "content": [
+            {"token_id": tid, "logprob": entry["logprob"], "top_logprobs": []}
+            for tid, entry in zip(choice["token_ids"], content)
+        ]
+    }
+

## Reproduction

- **Model**: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (`Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration`, hybrid GDN linear attention + full attention + sparse MoE)
- **LoRA adapter**: r=64, alpha=128, 780 keys, `target_parameters=[experts.gate_up_proj, experts.down_proj]`
- **GPU**: 8×H20-3e 144GB (Hopper sm_90), CUDA 13.0
- **vLLM**: 0.26.0 (cu130, torch 2.11.0+cu130)

## Symptoms

- **Short prompts**: LoRA works correctly (output differs from base model)
- **Long prompts** (>~128 tokens, e.g. 2335-char SciCode prompts): output becomes `!!!` (NaN), `/v1/completions` with `logprobs` returns `{"error":"Out of range float values are not JSON compliant: nan"}`

## Runtime Localization

Using `VLLM_ENABLE_V1_MULTIPROCESSING=0` + monkey-patching `Qwen3_5DecoderLayer.forward`:

1. **First NaN appears in layer 6** (GDN linear attention type), starting at **token 128**
2. All tokens from 128 onwards are NaN (346/474 tokens in a 474-token prefill)
3. `core_attn_out` (GDN attention core output) is NaN from token 128 — the NaN originates **inside** `torch.ops.vllm.qwen_gdn_attention_core`, not in the LoRA projection itself
4. LoRA weights are normal (max abs = 0.017, no NaN/inf) — **not a numerical overflow**
5. `linear_key_head_dim = 128`, `linear_value_head_dim = 128` — token 128 aligns with head_dim

The single-slice `lora_expand` kernel (used by GDN attention `out_proj` LoRA) gets `block_n = 128` from `get_lora_op_configs` (`64 if num_slices > 1 else 128`), which triggers the Hopper sm_90 NaN path.

## Fix

In `vllm/lora/ops/triton_ops/utils.py`, `get_lora_op_configs`, change the expand default:

```python
# Before:
"block_n": 64 if num_slices > 1 else 128,

# After:
"block_n": 64 if num_slices > 1 else 32,
```

## Verification

After the fix:
- Long prompts no longer produce NaN ✅
- 37-prompt LoRA effectiveness probe: 37/37 show output difference from base model ✅
- SciCode v51 training set (50 samples): **54.0% exact match, 95.1% avg similarity** — closely matching HF transformers + PEFT baseline (56.0% exact, 95.3% similarity)
- The ~2% gap is expected bf16 precision difference (vLLM Triton kernel vs torch matmul)

## Comparison with HF Transformers

Same adapter loaded via `PeftModel.from_pretrained` (transformers 5.5.3 + peft 0.19.1) produces **no NaN** on the same long prompts — confirming the bug is specific to vLLM's Triton `lora_expand` kernel, not the adapter weights.

## Note

We also found that `block_n=128` only triggers NaN for **single-slice** expand (GDN attention LoRA). Multi-slice expand (e.g. QKV projection) uses `block_n=64` and is unaffected. This is consistent with the issue title — the problem is specifically `block_n=128` on sm_90.

[Bug]: Split top-p mask kernel restarts its tie count every 8192 entries and over-keeps boundary ties

### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment (trimmed: only the kernel file matters)</summary>

```text
vLLM: vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py from upstream main @ fa75d3456d, loaded by path
      (the installed package also had PR 61996 applied, which changes nothing this file imports)
GPU: NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC (148 SMs), driver 580.178.04
PyTorch 2.14.0+cu132 (CUDA 13.2), Triton 3.8.0, Python 3.12.13, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
```

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

For top-p-only rows at batch <= 64 on CUDA, `apply_top_k_top_p_triton` uses the split top-p pipeline from #54651. Its mask kernel, `_topp_sb_mask_kernel`, keeps too many copies of the boundary value when those copies fall in more than one 8192-entry block of a slice.

The kernel keeps every token above the pivot, but of the copies of the boundary value `dup` it keeps only the first `numkeep`, in index order. A copy's rank is `num_preceding` (the copies in lower-indexed slices) plus its rank within the current block. The block loop never advances `num_preceding`, so the rank restarts at every block, and each block of the slice can keep up to `numkeep - num_preceding` copies on its own ([L1501-L1515](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa75d3456d60a5ffe923818c4b495295675b38e1/vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py#L1501-L1515)):

```python
for i in range(start, end, BLOCK):  # BLOCK=8192
    ...
    if ties:
        dmask = tl.exp(x - M) / Z == dup
        cum = tl.cumsum(dmask.to(tl.int32)).to(tl.float32) + num_preceding
        keep_dup = dmask & (cum <= numkeep)
        keep = keep & (~dmask | keep_dup)
        # missing: num_preceding += tl.sum(dmask.to(tl.float32))
```

The monolithic kernel carries the same count across its tiles (`num_kept += tl.sum(duplicate_keep_mask)`, [L874](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa75d3456d60a5ffe923818c4b495295675b38e1/vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py#L874)).

Scope:
- It only over-keeps. The extra tokens are all copies of the boundary value, so the kept set is still the top of the sorted row, but its mass can exceed `p` by up to the mass of the whole tie group instead of by less than one copy. Output stays deterministic.
- It needs slices longer than 8192 entries (`S < V / 8192`). At V=152576 on a 148-SM GPU, that holds for every batch of 5-64 rows (S <= 16).
- Exact ties at the boundary are common in real rows. bf16 logits have 8 significant bits, and in the real rows below, 550 of 1424 have more than one copy of the p=0.95 boundary value (up to 86 copies).

On 1424 real spec-decode verify rows from MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL (bf16-valued logits, V=152576, top_p=0.95, top-k rows at k=50) on B300, compared with a float64 top-p reference. The B=64 runs use the first 1408 rows (22 full batches).

| Batch (top-p-only + top-k rows) | S | Top-p-only rows | Rows with wrong kept count, main | With the fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B=64: 63 + 1 | 2 | 1386 | 327 (all over-keep) | 8 |
| B=64: 32 + 32 | 2 | 704 | 175 (all over-keep) | 4 |
| B=8: 7 + 1 | 16 | 1246 | 86 (all over-keep) | 13 |
| B=8: 4 + 4 | 16 | 712 | 45 (all over-keep) | 8 |

With every row at k=50, main has no wrong rows, so these counts come from the top-p-only rows. The rows that stay wrong with the fix are all over-keeps except one row at B=64 (63 + 1) that keeps fewer tokens, with kept mass no lower than p - 1e-6. I have not root-caused them; they are out of scope here.

**Repro.** Synthetic rows with 4096 exactly tied tokens at the boundary. The first half of the batch spreads them over 8 blocks of one slice; the second half packs the same values into one block. The script also loads a patched copy of the kernel file that advances the count:

    mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    sys.modules[name] = mod

    return mod

src = open(path).read()
old = "            keep = keep & (~dmask | keep_dup)\n"
assert src.count(old) == 1
new = old + "            num_preceding += tl.sum(dmask.to(tl.float32))\n"
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("w", suffix=".py", delete=False) as f:
    f.write(src.replace(old, new))
impls = {"main": load(path, "tt_main"), "main + fix": load(f.name, "tt_fix")}

x = torch.full((V,), -8.0)
x[V // 2:V // 2 + 64] = 4.0  # 64 tokens above the boundary

spread[0:V // 2:16] = 0.0  # 4096 tied tokens, 512 in each of 8 blocks
packed[0:8192:2] = 0.0  # the same 4096 tied tokens in one block

pp = torch.full((B,), p, device="cuda")
probs = torch.softmax(logits.double(), -1)

cum = probs[0].sort(descending=True).values.cumsum(0)

print(f"{torch.cuda.get_device_name()}: B={B} -> split top-p, S={S}, "

On 148 SMs at V=152576 it still uses S=16 (9536-entry slices) for B >= 5, the same S as the B=8 rows above.
